Lebesgue measure of distance sets and L2L^{2} ball inflationThanks: Bochen Liu was partially supported by the National Key R&D Program of China 2024YFA1015400. The draft of this paper was completed in March 2026. The authors acknowledge the use of generative AI tools for proof checking and typo correction.

Shengwen Gan Address: Department of Mathematics
Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, 510275, China Email address: shengwengan2018@gmail.com , Bochen Liu Address: Department of Mathematics & International Center for Mathematics, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen 518055, China Email address: Bochen.Liu1989@gmail.com and Shukun Wu Address: Department of Mathematics, Indiana University Bloomington, USA Email address: shukwu@iu.edu
Abstract.

We give an alternative proof of the 5/45/4 result of Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang on the Falconer distance conjecture: if a compact set EE in the plane has Hausdorff dimension >5/4>5/4, then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that the pinned distance set

Δx​(E):={|x−y|:y∈E}\Delta_{x}(E):=\{|x-y|:y\in E\}

has positive Lebesgue measure. Moreover, we are able to beat the 5/45/4 barrier if the packing dimension of EE is <2<2. More generally, we obtain sufficient conditions involving both the Hausdorff and packing dimensions of EE. These conditions improve the 5/45/4 threshold when the packing dimension of EE is <2<2, and recover the second author’s result for dimHE=dimPE>1\dim_{\textup{H}}E=\dim_{\textup{P}}E>1. The proof is based on L2L^{2} ball inflation and does not use decoupling inequalities.

Key words and phrases: 
Falconer’s distance problem, Hausdorff dimension, packing dimension
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
51E30, 28A75

1. Introduction

For a set E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}, define its distance set to be

Δ(E):={|x−x′|:x,x′∈E}.\Delta(E):=\{|x-x^{\prime}|:x,x^{\prime}\in E\}.

We also define the pinned distance set: For p∈ℝ2p\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, define

Δp​(E):={|x−p|:x∈E}.\Delta_{p}(E):=\{|x-p|:x\in E\}.

Let dimH\dim_{\textup{H}} denote the Hausdorff dimension, and dimP\dim_{\textup{P}} denote the packing dimension.

The goal of this paper is to prove the following result.

Theorem 1.1.

Let E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a compact set and let α=dimH(E)>1,β=dimP(E)\alpha=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)>1,\beta=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E). If

(1) α>32−12​β\alpha>\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2\beta}

and

(2) P⁡(α,β):=α3−(2​β−1)​α2−2​α+(3​β−1)<0,P(\alpha,\beta):=\alpha^{3}-(2\beta-1)\alpha^{2}-2\alpha+(3\beta-1)<0,

then there exists a point x∈Ex\in E such that the pinned distance set {|x−y|}y∈E\{|x-y|\}_{y\in E} has positive Lebesgue measure.

As a corollary, we recover the result of Guth, Iosevich, Ou and Wang [8].

Corollary 1.2.

If E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is compact and satisfies

dimH(E)>54,\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)>\frac{5}{4},

then there exists a point x∈Ex\in E such that the pinned distance set {|x−y|}y∈E\{|x-y|\}_{y\in E} has positive Lebesgue measure.

Proof.

Denote α:=dimH(E)>54,β:=dimP(E)\alpha:=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)>\frac{5}{4},\beta:=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E). Since β≤2\beta\leq 2, we have

α>54≥32−12​β.\alpha>\frac{5}{4}\geq\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2\beta}.

Noting that the coefficient of β\beta in P⁡(α,β)P(\alpha,\beta) is 3−2​α2<03-2\alpha^{2}<0 and β∈[α,2]\beta\in[\alpha,2], we have

P⁡(α,β)≤P⁡(α,α)=−α3+α2+α−1=−(α−1)2​(α+1)<0.P(\alpha,\beta)\leq P(\alpha,\alpha)=-\alpha^{3}+\alpha^{2}+\alpha-1=-(\alpha-1)^{2}(\alpha+1)<0.

By Theorem 1.1, the corollary holds. ∎

Remark 1.3.

It is surprising to us that our proof does not use decoupling, but nevertheless reaches the “54\frac{5}{4}-threshold”.

We also recover the equal Hausdorff/packing dimension case proved by the second author [12].

Corollary 1.4.

If E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is compact and satisfies

dimH(E)=dimP(E)>1,\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E)>1,

then there exists a point x∈Ex\in E such that the pinned distance set {|x−y|}y∈E\{|x-y|\}_{y\in E} has positive Lebesgue measure.

Proof.

Denote α:=dimH(E)=dimP(E)>1\alpha:=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E)>1. Then α>32−12​α\alpha>\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2\alpha}, and P⁡(α,α)=−(α−1)2​(α+1)<0P(\alpha,\alpha)=-(\alpha-1)^{2}(\alpha+1)<0. By Theorem 1.1, the corollary holds. ∎

If one wants to improve the 54\frac{5}{4}-threshold, one observes a specific structure in the set EE:

Corollary 1.5.

If E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a compact set satisfying dimH(E)=54\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)=\frac{5}{4} and |Δx​(E)|=0|\Delta_{x}(E)|=0 for all x∈Ex\in E, then dimP(E)=2\dim_{\textup{P}}(E)=2.

Proof.

Suppose β:=dimP(E)<2\beta:=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E)<2, then α:=dimH(E)=54>32−12​β\alpha:=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)=\frac{5}{4}>\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2\beta}. By Theorem 1.1, we must have

P⁡(54,β)≥0.P(\frac{5}{4},\beta)\geq 0.

However, P⁡(54,β)≤P⁡(54,54)<0P(\frac{5}{4},\beta)\leq P(\frac{5}{4},\frac{5}{4})<0, which is a contradiction. ∎

1.1. Historical results

Falconer [5] proved that if E⊂ℝdE\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is compact and dimH(E)>(d+1)/2\dim_{\mathrm{H}}(E)>(d+1)/2, then |Δ⁡(E)|>0|\Delta(E)|>0. He conjectured that the conclusion should hold under the hypothesis dimH(E)>d/2\dim_{\mathrm{H}}(E)>d/2. In the plane, Wolff [22] proved the result for dimH(E)>4/3\dim_{\mathrm{H}}(E)>4/3. In higher dimensions, Erdogan [4] proved it for dimH(E)>d/2+1/3\dim_{\mathrm{H}}(E)>d/2+1/3. Later, Du, Guth, Ou, Wang, Wilson, and Zhang [2], and Du and Zhang [3], developed weighted L2L^{2} restriction estimates and used them to obtain further progress on Falconer’s distance problem.

In 2019, the second author [11] proposed an L2L^{2} approach to the pinned distance set problem. A breakthrough was subsequently obtained by Guth, Iosevich, Ou, and Wang [8], who proved that if E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is compact and dimH(E)>5/4\dim_{\mathrm{H}}(E)>5/4, then |Δx​(E)|>0|\Delta_{x}(E)|>0 for some x∈Ex\in E. Their proof introduced the good-bad decomposition and applied decoupling inequalities to the distance set problem. This remains the best known threshold in dimension two.

The other direction on Falconer’s distance problem is to give a lower bound on the Hausdorff dimension of Δ​(E),Δx​(E)\Delta(E),\Delta_{x}(E) assuming dimH(E)>d2\dim_{H}(E)>\frac{d}{2}. In the plane, the best record was obtained by Stull [20], who used computability theory to show that dimH(E)>1\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)>1 implies dimH(Δx​(E))≥34\dim_{\textup{H}}(\Delta_{x}(E))\geq\frac{3}{4} for some x∈Ex\in E. Also, see the work of Katz and Tao [9], Bourgain [1], Wang and Zheng [21], Shmerkin [19], Keleti and Shmerkin [10], Shmerkin and Wang [16], Fiedler and Stull [6] [7]. In [6], Fiedler and Stull studied the distance problem taking into account both Hausdorff dimension and packing dimension. They proved that for E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with α=dimH(E)>1,β=dimP(E)\alpha=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)>1,\beta=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E), if β<(3+5)​α−1−52\beta<\frac{(3+\sqrt{5})\alpha-1-\sqrt{5}}{2}, then dim(Δx​(E))=1\dim(\Delta_{x}(E))=1 for some x∈Ex\in E. Comparing with Theorem 1.1, on the one hand, our conclusion is |Δx​(E)|>0|\Delta_{x}(E)|>0; on the other hand, we obtain some new range for the pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) (for example, (α,β)=(54,2−ε)(\alpha,\beta)=(\frac{5}{4},2-\varepsilon) is in our range but not in their range).

The distance set problem is also studied under some regularity assumption. See the work of Orponen [13] [14], Shmerkin [17] [18]. Very recently, the second author [12] proved that dimH(E)=dimP(E)>1\dim_{\textup{H}}(E)=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E)>1 implies |Δx​(E)|>0|\Delta_{x}(E)|>0 for some x∈Ex\in E. He introduced a multiscale good-bad decomposition and a multiscale Mizohata-Takeuchi-type estimate.

1.2. Structure of the paper

In Section 2, we sketch the proof of the main theorem. In Section 3, we introduce the terminology used throughout the paper. In Section 4, we prove a lemma for Lipschitz functions. In Section 5, we reduce Theorem 1.1 to Proposition 5.1. In Section 6, we perform the multiscale good-bad decomposition and estimate the bad part. In Section 7, we estimate the good part. In Section 8, we prove Theorem 1.1. Finally, in Section 9, we prove the weighted L2L^{2} estimate.

Similarly, we use A≈BA\approx B to denote A⪅BA\lessapprox B and B⪅AB\lessapprox A. 2. An overview of the proof

2.1. Weighted L2L^{2} estimate

The key task in the paper is to prove a weighted L2L^{2} estimate, which we formulate as follows.

Fix u∈[1,2]u\in[1,2]. Let X⊂B⁡(0,1)X\subset B(0,1) be a union of disjoint R−1R^{-1}-balls. We assume XX satisfies:

(3) |X∩B⁡(x,r)|≲R−2​(r​R)ufor any ​x∈B⁡(0,1)​ and ​R−1≤r≤1,|X|=R−2​Ru.\begin{split}&|X\cap B(x,r)|\lesssim R^{-2}(rR)^{u}\ \ \ \textup{for~any~}x\in B(0,1)\textup{~and~}R^{-1}\leq r\leq 1,\\ &|X|=R^{-2}R^{u}.\end{split}

(Here, |E||E| is the Lebesgue measure of the set EE.) Suppose F:ℝ2→ℂF:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} is any function with supp​F^⊂SR1\mathrm{supp}\widehat{F}\subset S^{1}_{R}, where SR1S^{1}_{R} is the circle of radius RR. We are interested in finding the smallest number D⁡(u)D(u) such that

(4) 1|X|​‖F‖L2​(X)2⪅RD⁡(u)​‖F‖L2​(B​(0,1))2\frac{1}{|X|}\|F\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lessapprox R^{D(u)}\|F\|_{L^{2}(B(0,1))}^{2}

holds for all R≥1R\geq 1 and X,FX,F as above. We use 𝐅⁡(u)\mathbf{F}(u) to denote the following statement.

𝐅⁡(u)\mathbf{F}(u): If E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a compact set of Hausdorff dimension greater than uu, then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) has positive Lebesgue measure.

To help understand the ideas, we will make several informal claims in this section without proofs. The rigorous proofs will be given in later sections.

We have the following implication from (4) to Falconer’s distance problem.

Claim 1.

Suppose (4) holds for D⁡(u)D(u) and D⁡(u)≤u−1D(u)\leq u-1, then 𝐅⁡(u)\mathbf{F}(u) holds.

Remark 2.1.

A classical weighted L2L^{2} estimate shows that (4) holds for D⁡(u)=1−u2D(u)=1-\frac{u}{2} (see, for example, [3, Corollary 1.7]). Plugging into D⁡(u)≤u−1D(u)\leq u-1, we see that 𝐅⁡(43)\mathbf{F}(\frac{4}{3}) holds. This corresponds to the result of Wolff [22].

It was observed by Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang [8] that one does not need the full strength of (4) in order to show 𝐅⁡(u)\mathbf{F}(u). Indeed, one may throw away the “bad” part of FF which can be handled by Orponen’s radial projection theorem [15], and prove an estimate for the remaining “good” part. Such an estimate suffices to derive 𝐅⁡(u)\mathbf{F}(u). The trick nowadays is known as the good-bad decomposition. Recently, the second author [12] introduced a multiscale good-bad decomposition, which we will adopt in this paper. Since it is too complicated to state here, we postpone the definition later. At present, we just use it as a black box and assume for any function FF as above, we have a multiscale good-bad decomposition

F=Fgood+Fbad.F=F_{\textup{good}}+F_{\textup{bad}}.

Here, FgoodF_{\textup{good}} is obtained from FF by throwing away some “heavy” wave packets. So, we can still assume supp​F^good⊂SR1\mathrm{supp}\widehat{F}_{\textup{good}}\subset S^{1}_{R} and ‖Fgood‖2≲‖F‖2\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{2}\lesssim\|F\|_{2}.

Similar to (4), we are now interested in

(5) 1|X|​‖Fgood‖L2​(X)2⪅RDgood​(u)​‖Fgood‖L2​(B​(0,1))2.\frac{1}{|X|}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lessapprox R^{D_{\textup{good}}(u)}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(B(0,1))}^{2}.

We have a similar implication:

Claim 2.

Suppose (5) holds for Dgood​(u)D_{\textup{good}}(u) and Dgood​(u)≤u−1D_{\textup{good}}(u)\leq u-1, then 𝐅⁡(u)\mathbf{F}(u) holds.

Remark 2.2.

Guth-Iosevich-Ou-Wang [8] proved that (5) holds for Dgood​(u)=2−u3D_{\textup{good}}(u)=\frac{2-u}{3}. Plugging into Dgood​(u)≤u−1D_{\textup{good}}(u)\leq u-1, we see that 𝐅⁡(54)\mathbf{F}(\frac{5}{4}) holds. Recently, the second author [12] showed that Dgood​(u)=0D_{\textup{good}}(u)=0 under the assumption that u>1u>1 and XX is AD-regular. (Here, AD-regular means |X∩B⁡(x,r)|∼R−2​(r​R)u|X\cap B(x,r)|\sim R^{-2}(rR)^{u} for all x∈Xx\in X and R−1≤r≤1R^{-1}\leq r\leq 1.)

2.2. Packing dimensions

To prove Theorem 1.1, we also need to incorporate the packing dimension. Recall that (3) is a discretized interpretation that XX has Hausdorff dimension ≥u\geq u. Now we introduce a discretized interpretation about the packing dimension.

Let |X|r|X|_{r} denote the smallest number of rr-balls needed to cover XX, also called the rr-covering number of XX. Let κ∈[u,2]\kappa\in[u,2]. In addition to (3), we also require XX to satisfy:

(6) |X|r≲r−κ​ for all ​R−1≤r≤1.|X|_{r}\lesssim r^{-\kappa}\textup{~for~all~}R^{-1}\leq r\leq 1.

We are interested in the following estimate:

(7) 1|X|​‖Fgood‖L2​(X)2⪅RDgood​(u,κ)​‖Fgood‖L2​(B​(0,1))2,\frac{1}{|X|}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lessapprox R^{D_{\textup{good}}(u,\kappa)}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(B(0,1))}^{2},

where XX satisfies (3) and (6). Denote the following statement:

𝐅⁡(u,κ)\mathbf{F}(u,\kappa): If E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a compact set of Hausdorff dimension greater than uu and packing dimension smaller than κ\kappa, then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) has positive Lebesgue measure.

We have the following informal results.

Claim 3.

Suppose (7) holds for Dgood​(u,κ)D_{\textup{good}}(u,\kappa) and Dgood​(u,κ)≤u−1D_{\textup{good}}(u,\kappa)\leq u-1, then 𝐅⁡(u,κ)\mathbf{F}(u,\kappa) holds.

Claim 4.

(7) holds for Dgood​(u,κ)=max⁡{κ−u2​κ−1,κ−u(u+1)​(2​κ−u−1)}D_{\textup{good}}(u,\kappa)=\max\{\frac{\kappa-u}{2\kappa-1},\frac{\kappa-u}{(u+1)(2\kappa-u-1)}\}. Therefore, by the previous Claim, 𝐅⁡(u,κ)\mathbf{F}(u,\kappa) holds if u>32−12​κu>\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2\kappa} and P⁡(u,κ)<0P(u,\kappa)<0.

2.3. Ball inflation process

We discuss the strategy to prove Claim 4. It is through a ball inflation process. Recall that XX is a union of R−1R^{-1}-balls satisfying (3) and (6). To pass from the left-hand side to the right-hand side in (7), we choose a sequence of scales 1=r0>r1>⋯>rk+1=R−11=r_{0}>r_{1}>\dots>r_{k+1}=R^{-1}. Let Nri​(X)N_{r_{i}}(X) be the rir_{i}-neighborhood of XX. We may morally view Nri​(X)N_{r_{i}}(X) as a union of rir_{i}-balls. Essentially, Nrk+1​(X)N_{r_{k+1}}(X) is XX and Nr0​(X)N_{r_{0}}(X) is B⁡(0,1)B(0,1). For each 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, we are going to prove an estimate

(8) 1|Nri​(X)|​‖Fgood‖L2​(Nri​(X))2⪅RDi​1|Nri−1​(X)|​‖Fgood‖L2​(Nri−1​(X))2.\frac{1}{|N_{r_{i}}(X)|}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(N_{r_{i}}(X))}^{2}\lessapprox R^{D_{i}}\frac{1}{|N_{r_{i-1}}(X)|}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(N_{r_{i-1}}(X))}^{2}.

Each time, the balls are inflated from radius rir_{i} to ri−1r_{i-1}. Combining all the estimates gives us

1|X|​‖Fgood‖L2​(X)2⪅RD1+⋯+Dk+1​‖Fgood‖L2​(B​(0,1))2.\frac{1}{|X|}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lessapprox R^{D_{1}+\dots+D_{k+1}}\|F_{\textup{good}}\|_{L^{2}(B(0,1))}^{2}.

Hence, our goal becomes to carefully choose a sequence {ri}\{r_{i}\} so as to minimize ∑i=1k+1Di\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}D_{i}.

Next, we will focus on the one-step ball inflation estimate (8). Before doing that we introduce some notation. First of all, we may assume XX satisfies the uniform property: For any R−1≤r≤1R^{-1}\leq r\leq 1, the quantities |Br∩X||B_{r}\cap X| are comparable for all dyadic rr-cubes BrB_{r} such that Br∩X≠∅B_{r}\cap X\neq\emptyset.

By the uniform property of XX, one may see that |X|r∼|X||Br∩X||X|_{r}\sim\frac{|X|}{|B_{r}\cap X|}. We define the branching function associated to XX to be f:[0,1]→[0,∞)f:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty) in the following way. For x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], let r=R−xr=R^{-x}. Then f⁡(x)f(x) is defined so that

|X|r∼Rf⁡(x).|X|_{r}\sim R^{f(x)}.

(Note that ff is defined up to an error about O⁡(1log⁡R)O(\frac{1}{\log R}).)

We summarize the properties of ff.

    ff is increasing; f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 since |X|1=1|X|_{1}=1; f⁡(1)=uf(1)=u since |X|R−1=R2​|X|=Ru|X|_{R^{-1}}=R^{2}|X|=R^{u}.

    Lip​(f)≤2\textup{Lip}(f)\leq 2. Indeed, for x′>xx^{\prime}>x, r=R−x,r′=R−x′r=R^{-x},r^{\prime}=R^{-x^{\prime}}, one has Rf⁡(x′)−f⁡(x)∼|X|r′|X|r∼|Br∩X||Br′∩X|≲|Br||Br′|∼R2​(x′−x)R^{f(x^{\prime})-f(x)}\sim\frac{|X|_{r^{\prime}}}{|X|_{r}}\sim\frac{|B_{r}\cap X|}{|B_{r^{\prime}}\cap X|}\lesssim\frac{|B_{r}|}{|B_{r^{\prime}}|}\sim R^{2(x^{\prime}-x)}.

Now we give the following definitions.

Definition 2.3.

Let ff be the branching function associated to XX. For [x1,x2]⊂[0,1][x_{1},x_{2}]\subset[0,1] and s∈[0,2]s\in[0,2], we say ff is ss-Frostman on [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] if for all x∈[x1,x2]x\in[x_{1},x_{2}],

f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x2)+s⁡(x−x2).f(x)\geq f(x_{2})+s(x-x_{2}).

Remark 2.4.

Our weighted L2L^{2} estimate is different from that proved by Du and Zhang [3]. Comparing with [3, (1.11)], our weighted L2L^{2} inequality contains a factor |X|R−1|X|_{R^{-1}} on the right hand side. Therefore, we are able to obtain some gain when the size of XX is small.

Ingredient 3 (A structure lemma for Lipschitz functions).

Suppose 1<u<κ≤21<u<\kappa\leq 2. Let f:[0,1]→[0,∞)f:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty) be a piecewise linear Lipschitz function satisfying: ff is increasing, f⁡(0)=0,f⁡(1)=uf(0)=0,f(1)=u, u​x≤f⁡(x)≤κ​xux\leq f(x)\leq\kappa x, Lip​(f)≤2\textup{Lip}(f)\leq 2. 3. Uniform measures and branching functions

In this section, we show that for a given measure, we can decompose it as a sum of uniform measures plus a negligible term. We also define the branching function for a uniform measure.

For a number 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1, we use 𝒟ρ={Qρ}\mathcal{D}_{\rho}=\{Q_{\rho}\} to denote the set of dyadic ρ\rho-cubes. In other words, each cube in 𝒟ρ\mathcal{D}_{\rho} is of form [n​ρ,(n+1)​ρ)×[m​ρ,(m+1)​ρ)[n\rho,(n+1)\rho)\times[m\rho,(m+1)\rho) for some n,m∈ℤn,m\in\mathbb{Z}. Throughout the paper, we fix a large integer TT, which will be determined later.

Given a sequence w=(w1,…,wT)∈[0,1]Tw=(w_{1},\dots,w_{T})\in[0,1]^{T} and R≫1R\gg 1, we say a measure ν\nu is (w;T)(w;T)-uniform at scale RR if for any 1≤i≤T1\leq i\leq T and any QR−iT∈𝒟R−iTQ_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}}\in\mathcal{D}_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}} with QR−iT∩supp​ν≠∅Q_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}}\cap\mathrm{supp}\nu\neq\emptyset, we have

ν⁡(QR−iT)∈[wi,2​wi).\nu(Q_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}})\in[w_{i},2w_{i}).

Next, we define the branching function of a uniform measure. Recall that ν\nu is (w;T)(w;T)-uniform at scale RR if for each 0≤i≤T0\leq i\leq T, ν\nu is supported in a union of dyadic R−iTR^{-\frac{i}{T}}-cubes, such that the mass of ν\nu in each such cube is ∼wi\sim w_{i}. Recall that |X|ρ|X|_{\rho} is the ρ\rho-covering number of XX. We may allow the measure to have total mass <1<1.

Definition 3.4 (Branching function).

Let ν\nu be a measure that is (w;T)(w;T)-uniform at scale RR, and is supported in [0,1)2[0,1)^{2}. Define f:[0,1]→[0,∞)f:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty) as follows.

For i∈{0,1,…,T}i\in\{0,1,\dots,T\}, define f⁡(iT)f(\frac{i}{T}) so that

|supp​ν|R−iT=Rf⁡(iT).|\mathrm{supp}\nu|_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}}=R^{f(\frac{i}{T})}.

Then define f⁡(x)f(x) by linearly interpolating the values {f⁡(iT)}\{f(\frac{i}{T})\}.

To be more flexible, we may define ff in the way that

|supp​ν|R−iT∼Rf⁡(iT).|\mathrm{supp}\nu|_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}}\sim R^{f(\frac{i}{T})}.

In this sense, the branching function is determined up to an error O⁡(1log⁡R)O(\frac{1}{\log R}), which is allowable for our use if RR is big enough.

It is easy to see ν([0,1)2)∼Rf⁡(iT)wi∼Rf⁡(iT)ν(QR−iT)\nu([0,1)^{2})\sim R^{f(\frac{i}{T})}w_{i}\sim R^{f(\frac{i}{T})}\nu(Q_{R^{-\frac{i}{T}}}) for each ii. For each x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], since xx is 1T\frac{1}{T}-close to some iT\frac{i}{T} and ff is 22-Lipschitz, we have

whenever QR−x∩supp​ν≠∅Q_{R^{-x}}\cap\mathrm{supp}\nu\neq\emptyset. If TT is large enough, then one may essentially view

ν(QR−x)∼ν([0,1)2)R−f⁡(x).\nu(Q_{R^{-x}})\sim\nu([0,1)^{2})R^{-f(x)}.

We recall the definition of Frostman/Katz-Tao conditions.

Definition 3.6.

Let f:[0,1]→[0,∞)f:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty) be a Lipschitz function. For [x1,x2]⊂[0,1][x_{1},x_{2}]\subset[0,1] and s∈[0,2]s\in[0,2], we say ff is ss-Frostman on [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] if for all x∈[x1,x2]x\in[x_{1},x_{2}],

f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x1)+s⁡(x−x1).f(x)\geq f(x_{1})+s(x-x_{1}).

We say ff is ss-Katz-Tao on [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] if for all x∈[x1,x2]x\in[x_{1},x_{2}],

f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x2)+s⁡(x−x2).f(x)\geq f(x_{2})+s(x-x_{2}).

For 0<γ≪s0<\gamma\ll s, we say ff is ss-Frostman with error γ\gamma on [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] if for all x∈[x1,x2]x\in[x_{1},x_{2}],

f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x1)+s⁡(x−x1)−γ.f(x)\geq f(x_{1})+s(x-x_{1})-\gamma.

We say ff is ss-Katz-Tao with error γ\gamma on [x1,x2][x_{1},x_{2}] if for all x∈[x1,x2]x\in[x_{1},x_{2}],

f⁡(x)≥f⁡(x2)+s⁡(x−x2)−γ.f(x)\geq f(x_{2})+s(x-x_{2})-\gamma.

If ff is ss-Frostman (resp. ss-Katz-Tao) with error γ\gamma on [0,1][0,1], we simply say ff is ss-Frostman (resp. ss-Katz-Tao) with error γ\gamma.

For a measure ν\nu that is (w;T)(w;T)-uniform at scale RR, we say ν\nu is ss-Frostman (resp. ss-Katz-Tao) if its branching function is ss-Frostman (resp. ss-Katz-Tao).

The next lemma tells us that we can partition an ss-Frostman measure into several measures that are both ss-Frostman and ss-Katz-Tao, up to small errors.

Lemma 3.7.

Suppose 0<γ≪s0<\gamma\ll s. Let ν\nu be a measure that is (w;T)(w;T)-uniform at scale RR and is ss-Frostman with error γ\gamma. Then there are M∼|supp​ν|R−1Rs−C​γM\sim\frac{|\mathrm{supp}\nu|_{R^{-1}}}{R^{s-C\gamma}} measures ν(1),…,ν(M)\nu^{(1)},\dots,\nu^{(M)} such that each ν(j)\nu^{(j)} is ss-Frostman up to an exponent error C​γ+O⁡(1/log⁡R)C\gamma+O(1/\log R) with uniform comparability constant, and satisfies |supp​ν(j)|R−1∼Rs−C​γ|\mathrm{supp}\nu^{(j)}|_{R^{-1}}\sim R^{s-C\gamma}. Also, ν=∑j=1Mν(j)\nu=\sum_{j=1}^{M}\nu^{(j)}. Moreover, in the comparability convention of the preceding remark, all ν(j)\nu^{(j)} admit a common branching profile f~\widetilde{f} with f~​(iT)=min⁡{f⁡(iT),s−C​γ}\widetilde{f}(\frac{i}{T})=\min\{f(\frac{i}{T}),s-C\gamma\} and |suppν(j)|R−i/T∼Rf~​(i/T)|\mathrm{supp}\nu^{(j)}|_{R^{-i/T}}\sim R^{\widetilde{f}(i/T)}. Here, CC is a universal constant.

Proof.

Let XX be the union of cubes in 𝒟R−1\mathcal{D}_{R^{-1}} that intersect supp​ν\mathrm{supp}\nu. Let ff be the branching function of ν\nu. Then

|X|R−xi∼Rf⁡(xi)|X|_{R^{-x_{i}}}\sim R^{f(x_{i})}

for 0≤i≤T0\leq i\leq T. Here we let xi=iTx_{i}=\frac{i}{T}. That ff is ss-Frostman with error γ\gamma means f⁡(x)≥s​x−γf(x)\geq sx-\gamma. We need to modify ff so that its value at x=1x=1 is s−C​γs-C\gamma.

More precisely, our goal is to find a partition X=⨆j=1MX(j)X=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^{M}X^{(j)} such that for each jj,

for 0≤i≤T0\leq i\leq T. Then we just set ν(j)=ν|X(j)\nu^{(j)}=\nu|_{X^{(j)}} and finish the proof.

Next, we construct these X(j)X^{(j)}. First, let ii be the minimal index such that |X|R−xi>Rs−C​γ|X|_{R^{-x_{i}}}>R^{s-C\gamma}. For each Q′∈𝒟R−xi−1Q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{R^{-x_{i-1}}} such that Q′∩X≠∅Q^{\prime}\cap X\neq\emptyset, we equally divide X∩Q′X\cap Q^{\prime} into A∼Rf⁡(xi)−s+C​γA\sim R^{f(x_{i})-s+C\gamma} pieces

4. A structure lemma for Lipschitz functions

In this section, we prove a structure lemma for Lipschitz functions. For convenience, we make the following definitions.

Definition 4.1 (Admissible interval).

For [a,b]⊂[0,1][a,b]\subset[0,1], we say [a,b][a,b] is admissible if 1−a≤2​(1−b)1-a\leq 2(1-b).

Definition 4.2.

Let f:[0,1]→ℝf:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}. If there exists 0=a0<a1<⋯<aM=10=a_{0}<a_{1}<\dots<a_{M}=1 such that f|[ai−1,ai]f|_{[}a_{i-1},a_{i}] is linear for all 1≤i≤M1\leq i\leq M, then we say ff is piecewise linear with MM pieces. Each [ai−1,ai][a_{i-1},a_{i}] is called an ff-piece.

The main result is as follows.

Lemma 4.3.

Let 1<u≤κ≤21<u\leq\kappa\leq 2. Then there exists ε⁡(u,κ)>0\varepsilon(u,\kappa)>0 such that for any 0<ε<ε⁡(u,κ)0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon(u,\kappa), the following holds. Let f:[0,1]→[0,∞)f:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,\infty) be a piecewise linear function, satisfying: ff is increasing, f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0, f⁡(1)=uf(1)=u, u​x≤f⁡(x)≤κ​xux\leq f(x)\leq\kappa x, Lip​(f)≤2\textup{Lip}(f)\leq 2. Then there exists a sequence 0=x0<x1<⋯<xk<xk+1=10=x_{0}<x_{1}<\dots<x_{k}<x_{k+1}=1 such that

  1. (1)

    For 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq{k}, ff is (1+ε)(1+\varepsilon)-Frostman on [xi−1,xi][x_{i-1},x_{i}] and [xi−1,xi][x_{i-1},x_{i}] is admissible.

  2. (2)

    f⁡(xk)=(2​κ−1)​xk−κ+1+O⁡(ε)f(x_{k})=(2\kappa-1)x_{k}-\kappa+1+O(\varepsilon).

  3. (3)

    At most C⁡(ε,u,κ)C(\varepsilon,u,\kappa) of the selected endpoints x0,…,xkx_{0},\dots,x_{k} are not endpoints of the given ff-pieces. In particular, k≤#⁡{f​-pieces}+C⁡(ε,u,κ)k\leq\#\{f\textup{-pieces}\}+C(\varepsilon,u,\kappa) for some C⁡(ε,u,κ)C(\varepsilon,u,\kappa).

Proof.

We first draw a graph as in Figure 1. The coordinates of marked points are:

  1. (1)

    O=(0,0)O=(0,0);

  2. (2)

    P=(1,0)P=(1,0);

  3. (3)

    E=(uκ,u)E=(\frac{u}{\kappa},u);

  4. (4)

    F′=(u+κ−12​κ−1,u)F^{\prime}=(\frac{u+\kappa-1}{2\kappa-1},u);

  5. (5)

    G=(1,u)G=(1,u);

    I′=(κ−12​κ−u−1,u⁡(κ−1)2​κ−u−1)I^{\prime}=(\frac{\kappa-1}{2\kappa-u-1},\frac{u(\kappa-1)}{2\kappa-u-1});

One can also check the following property. 5. A standard reduction

We first make a standard reduction to Theorem 1.1. Recall that α=dimH(E),β=dimP(E)\alpha=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E),\beta=\dim_{\textup{P}}(E). Without loss of generality, we assume E⊂[0,1)2E\subset[0,1)^{2} and there exist E1,E2⊂EE_{1},E_{2}\subset E so that dist​(E1,E2)≳1\textup{dist}(E_{1},E_{2})\gtrsim 1 and dimH(E1)=dimH(E2)=α\dim_{\textup{H}}(E_{1})=\dim_{\textup{H}}(E_{2})=\alpha. 9. Weighted L2L^{2} estimate

Let σS\sigma_{S} be the surface measure on the unit circle SS, and we define the extension operator E:S→ℝ2E:S\to\mathbb{R}^{2} as

(79) E​f​(x)=∫ei​x⋅ξ​f​(ξ)​d​σS​(ξ).Ef(x)=\int e^{ix\cdot\xi}f(\xi)d\sigma_{S}(\xi).

Consider also its “broad” variant:

Definition 9.1.

Let K≥1K\geq 1 and A∈ℕA\in\mathbb{N}. Let Σ={σ}\Sigma=\{\sigma\} be a set of 2-overlapping K−1K^{-1}-arcs that covers SS. Let fσ=f​𝟏σf_{\sigma}=f\boldsymbol{1}_{\sigma}. For any f:S→ℂf:S\to\mathbb{C} and x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, define

(80) BrA​E​f​(x):=maxΣ′⊂Σ,#​Σ′=A⁡minσ∈Σ′​|E​fσ​(x)|.{\rm{Br}}_{A}Ef(x):=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\Sigma^{\prime}\subset\Sigma,\\ \#\Sigma^{\prime}=A\end{subarray}}\min_{\sigma\in\Sigma^{\prime}}|Ef_{\sigma}(x)|.

We also recall the classical definition of a Katz-Tao (R−1,s)(R^{-1},s)-set.

Definition 9.2.

Let R>1R>1, s>0s>0. Let X⊂B⁡(0,1)X\subset B(0,1) be a disjoint union of R−1R^{-1}-balls. We say XX is a Katz-Tao (R−1,s,C)(R^{-1},s,C)-set if

|X∩B⁡(x,r)|≤C​R−2​(r​R)s|X\cap B(x,r)|\leq CR^{-2}(rR)^{s}

for any B⁡(x,r)B(x,r). When CC is a fixed large constant, we simply say XX is a Katz-Tao (R−1,s)(R^{-1},s)-set.

Lemma 9.3.

Let X⊂BRX\subset B_{R} be a union of unit balls such that the R−1R^{-1}-dilate of XX is a Katz-Tao (R−1,s)(R^{-1},s)-set. Then for all ε>0\varepsilon>0,

Consequently, we obtain

The proof relies on the standard broad-narrow reduction and the bilinear restriction theorem. See [23] for a similar argument. For a given ε\varepsilon in (81), pick K=Rε2K=R^{\varepsilon^{2}} and A=8A=8 in Definition 9.1. Clearly, we have

‖E​f‖L2​(X)2≲KO⁡(1)​‖Br8​E​f‖L2​(X)2≲RO⁡(ε2)​∑σ1,σ2∈Σ,dist​(σ1,σ2)≥K−1∫X|E​fσ1​E​fσ2|.\|Ef\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lesssim K^{O(1)}\|\mathrm{Br}_{8}Ef\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lesssim R^{O(\varepsilon^{2})}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\Sigma,\\ \textup{dist}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\geq K^{-1}\end{subarray}}\int_{X}|Ef_{\sigma_{1}}Ef_{\sigma_{2}}|.

Via Cauchy-Schwarz, we have

∑σ1,σ2∈Σ,dist​(σ1,σ2)≥K−1∫X|E​fσ1​E​fσ2|≲|X|1/2​∑σ1,σ2∈Σ,dist​(σ1,σ2)≥K−1(∫X|E​fσ1​E​fσ2|2)1/2,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\Sigma,\\ \textup{dist}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\geq K^{-1}\end{subarray}}\int_{X}|Ef_{\sigma_{1}}Ef_{\sigma_{2}}|\lesssim|X|^{1/2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\Sigma,\\ \textup{dist}(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2})\geq K^{-1}\end{subarray}}\Big(\int_{X}|Ef_{\sigma_{1}}Ef_{\sigma_{2}}|^{2}\Big)^{1/2},

which, by using the bilinear restriction theorem, is bounded above by

KO⁡(1)​|X|1/2​∑σ1,σ2∈Σ‖fσ1‖2​‖fσ2‖2≲KO⁡(1)​|X|1/2​‖f‖22≲KO⁡(1)​|X|ss+1​‖f‖22.K^{O(1)}|X|^{1/2}\sum_{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}\in\Sigma}\|f_{\sigma_{1}}\|_{2}\|f_{\sigma_{2}}\|_{2}\lesssim K^{O(1)}|X|^{1/2}\|f\|_{2}^{2}\lesssim K^{O(1)}|X|^{{\frac{s}{s+1}}}\|f\|_{2}^{2}.

Since K=Rε2K=R^{\varepsilon^{2}}, the above calculations show that

‖E​f‖L2​(X)2≲RO⁡(ε2)​|X|ss+1​‖f‖22.∎\|Ef\|_{L^{2}(X)}^{2}\lesssim R^{O(\varepsilon^{2})}|X|^{{\frac{s}{s+1}}}\|f\|_{2}^{2}.\qed
